newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq appears to pull back, Kurds keep battling.
newsitem.headline: Iraq appears to pull back, Kurds keep battling.

text.p: Kurdish factions in northern Iraq clashed near the Iranian border and a strategic road to Sulaimaniya but the United States said it was satisfied that Iraqi troops were withdrawing from the area.

The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), which a week ago took the regional city of Arbil with help from Iraqi forces, struck at Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) positions in five villages around Halabja, 10 km (six miles) from the border, a PUK official said.
"But with the support of new forces moved into position, control of three of the villages was regained late last night," Shorsh Jalalal told Reuters in Sulaimaniya, the PUK stronghold.

The PUK said KDP and Iraqi forces had started to advance from Arbil along the north route towards Sulaimaniya via Degala and the key town of Koi Sanjaq. Control of Degala would command the other main route to Sulaimaniya and cut it off from Arbil.
Adnan Mufti, a PUK central committee member, said the Iraqi army controlled positions more than 20 km (12 miles) from Arbil, including parts of one main road to Sulaimaniya.

But U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said Washington was satisfied Iraqi troops were leaving Kurdish areas after their offensive into the safe haven set up for Kurds in northern Iraq by the U.S.-led alliance after the 1991 Gulf war.
Asked by reporters in Washington if he was satisfied with the withdrawal of Iraq President Saddam Hussein's forces from northern Iraq, Perry said: "So far, so good."
The Iraqi military intervention prompted U.S. retaliation earlier this week, with cruise missile attacks on air defence targets in southern Iraq.
A U.S. Defence Department spokesman said the air strikes destroyed or damaged up to 11 of the 15 targets and "achieved a severe degradation of Iraq defences south of the 33rd parallel."
President Bill Clinton said earlier the raids had achieved his goal of forcing Iraqi forces to withdraw from the Kurdish haven in the north.

Turkish officials said the volatility in northern Iraq had forced them to consider establishing a temporary security cordon on the border to stop Turkish Kurdish rebels from infiltrating into southeastern Turkey.

"We have security problems at our borders," Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said. "Each time this kind of military action happens, the terrorists build up on our borders and then try to infiltrate. So we need this security zone there."

Turkish Foreign Ministry officials said "conditions" would determine how long the cordon would remain and how many troops would patrol the zone, set to extend up to 10 km (six miles) into northern Iraq.
An Iraqi Foreign Ministry official, Saad al-Faisel, said on state-run television that Baghdad had protested against the Turkish plan.
"We formally and categorically reject it. We shall not accept this because it constitutes a violation of Iraq's sovereignty. It is unacceptable and we have informed the Turks of this," he said.
The United States said it backed the Turkish idea but France, which failed to support the cruise missile attacks or a U.S. decision to extend a no-fly zone over southern Iraq, condemned the plan.
